title: Seven Lessons from the “Impossible” Ridglan Rescue
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: The rescue at Ridglan Farms should have been an impossible mission. I first broached the idea with experienced activists in late 2025, shortly after special prosecutor Tim Gruenke announced that, despite clear evidence of felony animal abuse at the facility, he would take no action to help the dogs. My immediate reaction: “If the government won’t save them, we will.” Come hang out with me tomorrow at 7 pm in Berkeley! I’m in the Bay Area and hosting a short talk and hangout tomorrow (Monday, November 2) at the Berkeley Animal Rights Center at 7 pm for anyone interested in the Ridglan campaign! RSVP here . But virtually all the veteran activists I talked to told me to forget about it. Ridglan had a barbed wire fence and was on high alert for activists. Years of prosecutions had depleted the open rescue movement of leaders. And the local authorities in Dane County were co-opted by the industry; the special prosecutor bent over backwards to cater to the industry, for example, while refusing to even talk to any of the witnesses of animal abuse at Ridglan Farms. The system was broken and corrupt. That left us facing seemingly impossible odds. But we took on the mission anyway. And we won. Every one of the Ridglan dogs is now free. Now, just 7 months later, we face another daunting challenge: rescuing the 16,000 dogs at Marshall BioResources. Once again, people are saying it is an impossible mission, despite disturbing evidence of criminal abuse. Dogs at Marshall are injected with toxins that leave them thrashing and screaming, as if they are being “ burned alive from the inside ,” according to one witness. Marshall in North Rose is even more fiercely guarded than Ridglan—razor wire apparently covers the grounds of the facility—and it has enormous political influence that protects it from accountability. But the Marshall rescue can nonetheless be done. In fact, it must be done. To pull it off, however, we have to learn the lessons from Ridglan. Here are some of the important ones. Lesson 1: Open rescue can create transformative change—under the right conditions. Open rescue fulfills the two most important goals of any strategy for social change: attention and sympathy. But at Ridglan, we learned two very important lessons about the conditions in which open rescue works. The first condition is transparency. We not only declined to hide our faces at the March rescue. We openly announced we were going to do it months before the action. This allowed us to recruit from a much wider pool of people. It built a dramatic storyline as the date of the rescue approached. And it furthered our case that we have the legal right to rescue animals from abuse. After all, why hide an action if it’s within your legal rights? The other very important lesson is that numbers matter. The training, communication, and legal support required of mass actions is an enormous project. But unlike many movement leaders, I thought the evidence from the last 10 years showed mass actions were worth the effort. Effective movements are, in no small part, simply a numbers game. Ridglan showed the power of those numbers. Lesson 2: Find the BHAG. Historically, big goals have been looked upon with suspicion by the animal movement. The vast majority of the effort and resources go to campaigns that make small, incremental asks—bigger cages or better deaths. In contrast, the Ridglan case had Big Hairy Audacious Goals (BHAG). We not only said we were going to rescue every last one of the Ridglan dogs. We talked about how we were going to save all the animals cruelly used in experiments. Outside of the animal context, BHAGs are widely understood to be crucial to making big progress. Google’s CEO has spoken about why his company almost always sets ambitious, “moonshot” goals. Big goals inspire the most high impact people to join the effort. Extraordinary people want to work on extraordinary things. Ridglan recruited countless extraordinary people to do something big together. Lesson 3: Leadership requires soft skills, not charisma. Traditionally, people think of leaders as charismatic, extroverted, and great speakers. The leaders of the Ridglan campaign were different. Team leads were chosen based mostly on character traits, not charisma. Can this person handle conflict well? Will this person remain nonviolent? Can this person engage effectively with large numbers of people, some of whom will be very different from who they are? These soft leadership skills are increasingly important in a world where movements are built from decentralized social networks, rather than traditional political structures or community organizations (such as churches). These soft skills are particularly important when leaders are asking people to take on risk. Recent research shows that one of the most important attributes of leadership is the ability to quickly appreciate tradeoffs in activism. If people are going to take risks, they want to know that their leaders are able to appreciate the costs and benefits of each course of action. (Interestingly, the worst leaders were the ones who nominated themselves to be leaders!) But as trust declines, and communities deteriorate, leaders aren’t just responsible for making good decisions. They’re responsible for building mini-communities. It’s the only way to ensure that hard decisions, with difficult trade-offs, are supported. Lesson 4: AI is a game changer—but only if you’re obsessed. AI was a massive force amplifier throughout the Ridglan campaign. We used it to research Ridglan and its buyers. We used it to build websites. We even used it to manage conflict resolution processes. What we consistently found, however, is that people differed dramatically in their ability to use AI effectively. Those who were highly committed to it could produce vastly more output: multiple 20-page legal briefs in a single day; world class websites in minutes; and training documents that were clear, concise, and grounded in scientific evidence. But when we tried to scale up the use of AI, it generally fell flat. The vast majority of people could not or would not use it effectively. This is consistent with research on AI’s learning function in randomized experiments. Overall, it seems to improve expertise, but this improvement is focused on those who are top performers . Lesson 5: To win, you need skill at the outside and inside game. Most animal rights groups try to play outside (grassroots, protest, direct action) or inside (lobbying, persuasion, negotiation). We did both, and it worked. The campaign started with direct action, the open rescue of dogs in 2017. But then it moved to the inside game. Petitioning the government for a special prosecutor and passing local legislation. Combining the inside and outside games is something that successful social movements, such as the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, did extremely well. We are learning to do the same. Lesson 6: Pitch a tent so big it’s a little uncomfortable. In a world that’s highly polarized, it’s hard to build a large, diverse grassroots movement. People immediately attack one another for political differences. But that’s precisely what movements need: numbers create power, and diversity shows that power is not a niche element of society. To solve this problem, we went out of our way to say, “We are building a tent so big it would make you a little uncomfortable.” The result was a movement that had leftist Jen Welch and MAGA influencer Lara Trump in the same coalition. To win at Marshall, we’ll have to pitch a similarly big tent. Lesson 7: Delete the rules. Focus on values. Scale usually requires bureaucracy. And bureaucracy kills initiative and flexibility. When people see hard rules that clearly don’t work, they get frustrated and leave. As much as possible, we tried to eliminate these rules, and the many other permission structures that frustrate movements as they scale up, and focus instead on shared values. 1 For example, our code of conduct was two words: be cool. For another, we rarely, if ever, told people not to take a certain course of action. Instead, we just asked them a values-based question: “Is your action nonviolent?” To get the speed and scale necessary to save the dogs at Marshall, we’ll have to take a similar approach. What else is going on? Preliminary hearings and arraignment for 47 new defendants in the Ridglan case. Last week, the state brought burglary charges against a large number of additional defendants. I’ll have more to say about the case later this week. For now, this is the highlight: the prosecution is on the defensive, and it showed. My wife Rose is on trial this week for attempting to protect horses from abuses in the racing industry. She and around 100 other animal activists nonviolently attempted to enter the track and sit on the field peacefully before the Grand National. The authorities arrested her and charged her with conspiracy. They did nothing about the abuses at the track, despite the fact that a horse died in a race within an hour of their demonstration. This will be a very hard case, but I believe in my wife—and the compassion of the people of Britain. I won’t be personally joining this trial, as I’m on doggie care duty (and the trial is very far from London in Liverpool). But I’ll be following it closely and providing updates on X/Twitter. We should be announcing a new strategy to save the Marshall dogs soon. I and a number of other committed organizers and partners in the campaign to stop the abuses at Marshall, and get all the dogs out, have been in intensive meetings for the last couple days. We hope to announce a new strategic framework for the campaign within a week. That’s all for now! 1 Interestingly, recent research into artificial intelligence alignment suggests there’s merit to this approach in other forms of complex systems. AI trained on principles seems to be better aligned than AI trained on a fixed set of rules.

title: This Pharma Giant Injected Dogs With Rabies. Here’s Why It’s a Threat to You.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: In November 2025, Merck quietly published results from an experiment where it injected rabies into dozens of Ridglan dogs, watched them descend into fear and madness, then cut out their brain tissue to vivisect. Just one month earlier, in October of 2025, Ridglan had been implicated in hundreds of new counts of felony animal abuse. The state Veterinary Examining Board (VEB) was so shocked by the cruelty at Ridglan, including dogs being surgically mutilated without anesthesia, that it issued an order indicating that the situation at Ridglan “imperatively requires emergency action.” The VEB did its part to respond to the emergency; it suspended the license of Rick Van Domelen, the veterinarian and facility manager at Ridglan Farms. It was the only suspension the VEB would issue for the entire year of 2025. Yet despite the official findings of animal abuse, and the mass outcry against Ridglan, there was one Ridglan customer who continued to shamelessly work with the company: Merck. Merck published its November 2025 study, which it had collaborated with Ridglan on, then it went back to Ridglan for even more dogs in 2026. As recently as May of this year, Merck was still buying dogs from Ridglan. The entire nation said the abuse must stop, from Lara Trump to Ricky Gervais. Merck ensured it would continue. Here, however, is the key point. The cruelty inflicted on those defenseless dogs is not just an animal welfare issue. It is a demonstration of something much darker: a political system that allows the most powerful and wealthy interests to hurt or kill anyone—including you. If Big Pharma can get away with ruthlessly torturing puppies, it can get away with hurting you. That might seem like an exaggeration. It is not. Merck and other pharmaceutical companies have targeted, not just dogs, but human beings as test subjects for corporate profit. From the opioid crisis caused by Purdue Pharma to thousands of heart attack deaths caused (and covered up) by Merck’s Vioxx, drug companies have for many years covered up deadly outcomes in pursuit of profit. The consequences of this corruption are dire. In the case of Merck’s work with Ridglan, dogs in the rabies trials suffered from “sudden anorexia, signs of apprehension or nervousness,” “ataxia” (loss of motor function), and even “paralysis.” As a dog neared her death, “a normally docile [dog] may suddenly become vicious.” In the case of Merck’s work on the painkiller Vioxx, millions of Americans were duped into buying a deadly painkiller. As many as 100,000 people had heart attacks and died as a result. Despite a 2008 investigation by the Journal of the American Medical Association showing an intentional cover-up by Merck, no one at the company was ever criminally prosecuted. If a company is allowed to do horrifying, illegal things, it’s just a matter of time before it does horrible, illegal things to you. But here is the optimistic piece. Things are changing. Across the globe, people are recognizing the dangers posed by concentrated power in the hands of those who pursue profit above all else. Purdue Pharma, which followed in Merck’s footsteps by covering up the risks of another deadly painkiller, OxyContin, is now bankrupt and gone. Merck, if it does not reform, must be next. But as with Purdue, it won’t happen without exposure and grassroots effort. The regulators, too often, are bought by the corporations they are supposed to regulate. The politicians, too often, are wined and dined by the lobbyists. To protect the dogs—to protect all of us—it will take a movement. I hope you’ll join it this weekend. What’s up this week? The weekend of action to save the dogs is October 23-25. My friend Zoe and the grassroots animal rights network Direct Action Everywhere are leading the effort to protest companies like Merck, which experiment on dogs. You can find a list of protests to join—or even put together a protest yourself—at this website . Every person can make a difference, so even if you’ve never protested, make it out! The Ridglan prosecution escalated this week, with dozens of new people formally charged. Today, 48 new defendants had their initial appearance. The District Attorney himself, Ismael Ozanne, tried to argue that defendants should be held in custody unless they paid bail, and even asked for an ankle monitor to be placed on defendant Amy Van Aartsen. His arguments failed, and every defendant was released without bail. But this is just the start of a long fight against a corrupt prosecutorial establishment. We will defend the right to rescue, and, with your support, we will win. The COMPACT Act , which would ban federal funding of dog and cat experiments, is off to a great start. Jen, one of the leaders of the political effort at Save the Dogs, gave a great Zoom presentation this weekend about what’s going on with the Act, including the rapid recruitment of co-sponsors of the bill. Perhaps the most inspiring example of this is Claudia Tenney, the Republican House member whose district includes the notorious Marshall BioResources, the single largest dog breeding and experimentation facility in the nation. If you want to hear more about what’s going on, and why we are focused on the COMPACT Act, check out this video . Apologies for the decline in content. I keep trying to keep up with content creation. And I keep failing. My latest excuse is graduate school. But I am going to make another public commitment to publish much more regularly on this Substack. The goal will be at least two posts a week. Eventually, I may even try to go back to writing every day! That’s all for now!

title: Today, You Could Help Us End Experiments on Dogs. (Literally, Today.)
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: Nick Langworthy and Mark Pocan, with Save the Dogs Rebekah Robinson in the background at the recent press conference. On Wednesday, September 23, Rep. Mark Pocan and Rep. Nick Langworthy proposed legislation that could save tens of thousands of dogs from cruel experiments, the COMPACT Act . The legislation, which would end all NIH funding of experiments on cats and dogs, will kick off what will likely be the most important political fight in the history of animal experimentation. Billions of dollars are used by the federal government on unethical experiments. That entire ecosystem of lobbyists, contract researchers, and other beneficiaries of taxpayer handouts will fight tooth and nail to keep the money in place. It’s crucial we prepare for that fight. Today, the Save the Dogs coalition will have our first call to do just that—and Rep. Pocan will be joining us. Join our first call in the fight to pass the COMPACT Act tonight (September 27) at 8 pm ET / 5 pm PT —and learn from Rep. Pocan himself about what each of us can do to save the dogs trapped in labs. RSVP here and join at savethedogs.io/zoom . How do we ensure our campaign has maximum impact? Here are a few key lessons from the research. Authentic contact from constituents still makes a difference . A 2015 study shows that legislators who were randomly assigned to receive constituent calls on a policy issue were 12% more likely to support the policy. Legislators correctly assume that every person motivated enough to call probably represents 10x as many who support the policy. You can help us pass the COMPACT Act by making a call today. Consider making a small donation—then asking for a meeting with the senior legislative staff . David Broockman and Josh Kalla, two leading scholars who have been supportive of our work, found that senior legislative officials were 3-4 times as likely to meet with constituents who identified themselves as donors to local races. Give a small amount, even $10, and then tell the staffers you are a donor who would like to meet with the legislator (or their senior staff) about the bill. Have dinner with legislative staff rather than formal lobbying . Traditional forms of lobbying are rapidly diminishing in impact, as the sheer volume of lobbyists and issues has increased so rapidly. Meeting legislative staff for a meal—so-called “ social lobbying ,” which focuses on building a social tie rather than just a transactional political relationship—can lead to better results. Ask the staff of your House and Senate members if they can meet you for dinner. Empower the legislative staff to make the case for us . When outside groups made presentations to legislators, it had virtually no impact in one experiment. In contrast, when the same presentation was given by a legislator’s own staff, it increased the odds that the legislator would take the recommended position by 17% . When you meet with legislative staff over a meal, spend a lot of time listening—and empowering them to make the case with their boss. Join a protest—and build a movement. The most powerful political movements are fueled by direct action. Evidence shows that protests, at least if they reach a certain scale and salience, can shift legislators dramatically in the direction of the protest. But, interestingly, the mechanism may not be direct . Protests’ primary effect is to inspire a larger base of support for a movement, which in turn will contact legislators authentically and fuel a cycle of political change. Join an upcoming protest against Marshall BioResources or one of its buyers. These are just some of the tips we’ll be sharing with you on calls like the one being held today. But by far the most important factor in a campaign’s success is the number of people acting to support it. Every person counts, no matter how seemingly small the contribution. Don’t let perfection be the enemy of the good. Join the call today at 8 pm ET / 5 pm PT . And let’s find some way, no matter how seemingly small, to plug you in. Then let’s go save some dogs.

title: My Wife Was Convicted for Rescuing Lambs. Here’s Why I’m More Hopeful Than Ever.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: My wife Rose in the foreground, with her co-defendant Sarah Foy in the background with lambs at the estate of King Charles. On Thursday, my wife Rose Patterson was convicted by a jury for rescuing three lambs from the King of England. When the verdict was spoken by the foreman of the jury—a stern-faced man who scowled through most of the trial—it hit me like a truck. We had been hopeful about the outcome of the trial, despite chaos in the court schedule (and thus our preparations). A juror in the front row, an older woman with short brown hair and glasses, had given what seemed like a wink to the defendants just a day before. But it was not the sign I thought it was. That same woman, as she walked into the courtroom for the verdict, gave out a visible sigh, as if she had given up on the case. Moments later, we heard the cursed words. “Guilty!” the foreman said, with acid in his voice. He repeated two more times for the other defendants. We did not know at the time what sentence would be imposed. And while the “theft” of a lamb—a nonviolent action done with good intentions—would not usually be hit with severe sentences, recent activist cases have led to shockingly harsh punishments in the UK. Two young women were sentenced to 20 and 24 months for splashing tomato soup on the glass case of a Van Gogh painting in the National Gallery. Palestine Action protesters were hit with sentences of 4-7 years for doing damage to an Israeli arms contractor based in the UK. Sentences against nonviolent protesters have become so severe in recent years that Human Rights Watch and a UN Special Rapporteur have condemned the UK’s crackdown on activists as a threat to democracy. We didn’t know if Rose and her co-defendants Rosa Sharkey and Sarah Foy would become yet another case study in a human rights organization’s report on the rise of authoritarianism in Europe. And yet I remain more optimistic than ever. This is partly because their case is bringing attention to the abuse of animals. Even conservative outlets, such as the Daily Mail , gave extensive coverage to the concerns raised by my wife about animals being improperly stunned on the slaughter line—leaving many to be effectively eviscerated alive. But the primary reason I’m optimistic is that, no matter what happens in this one case, it does not change that “the writing is on the wall.” Those are the words of another man who attempted to put my wife in prison in a very similar case. Scott Marshall, the CEO and patriarch of Marshall BioResources, said those words in an article recently about the March to Abolish Animal Testing, which ended today at the front gates of the massive Marshall facility in North Rose, NY, where over 16,000 dogs are caged and prepared for experiments. “For many years we never had protests at our sites,” Marshall said. “Now within last couple years due to our main competitors going out of business, we’re the last man standing and we’re a big target.” “Nobody wants to see dogs used in research,” Marshall continued. “I know the writing is on the wall.” And he is right—about all forms of animal abuse. Earlier this year, my wife Rose was acquitted in a case very similar to her lamb trial. Two other cases involving farm animals ended in historic acquittals in the United States. Those court cases, however, are just one part of a much larger change that is coming for companies like Marshall. In the last week, a former prosecutor we are working with, Bonnie Klapper, has had productive conversations with influential members of government regarding the criminal referral she submitted last month regarding mass killings at Marshall. A criminal case may actually be brought against Marshall—an unprecedented development against a large corporate abuser. Perhaps even more important, funding for the entire industry may soon end. On Wednesday, September 23, House members Nick Langworthy (NY) and Mark Pocan (WI) introduced bipartisan legislation, the COMPACT Act, that would end all NIH funding of experiments on dogs and cats. It is a courageous, historic proposal—and one that will effectively defund the entire industry, which depends on NIH funding to prop up its criminal activities, including not just mass killings but devocalization surgeries, inhalation experiments, and worse. The industry is fighting back so hard precisely because it is under duress. That is a reason for hope. For this hope to be realized, though, we need a movement to rise up. One of the saddest things about my wife’s court case was that, while there was extensive media, the courtroom was mostly empty of supporters. On the first day of the trial, journalists outnumbered me (the sole supporter in the gallery). There was little pressure on the court or government to give my wife a fair shot. This short circuits the power of direct action, which creates change by mobilizing support for the cause through symbolism and sacrifice. Things will be very different in the fight for the dogs. Already, Reps. Langworthy and Pocan have shown their support not just for their legislation—but for the rescue efforts by the movement. Langworthy was outside the gates of Marshall himself just a few months ago demanding freedom for the dogs. Pocan joined the Ridglan rescuers at a reunion for the Ridglan beagles, even as many faced criminal charges. (He took a photo with the defendants.) Support from Congress members such as Pocan and Langworthy will destabilize the industry’s efforts to tarnish us as radicals and criminals; we have the support of the very figures elected to represent the public will. But to sustain that support—to sustain the rising movement— we need you to support them, the legislators and the dogs. On Sunday, Sept 27, Mark Pocan will be joining us to talk about the COMPACT Act—and what you can do to help pass it. It is a relationship that is crucial not just for saving the dogs and cats, but countless future animals, too. So I hope you will join us. Numbers really count. You can RSVP here for the call, which will be 8 pm ET / 5 pm PT at savethedogs.io/zoom . It is too late for my wife and her co-defendants. I am partly to blame for that, as I did precious little to assist her legal defense (or promote her story) in the weeks and months leading up to the trial. And yet, even in her case, the ending was not as harsh as we feared. “I believe this case is suitable for a community order,” the Judge indicated at sentencing. He described the three defendants as “intelligent and capable women” who were raising “sensitive and important matters of public interest.” They will each do 150 hours of community service and pay a £250 fine but serve no jail time. History will remember even this light punishment very differently. Today’s criminals are tomorrow’s freedom fighters. Three sheep, whose lives would have ended in terror in a slaughterhouse, remain alive because of my wife’s courage. The same will soon be said about the dogs at Marshall BioResources. One person’s courage—to make a phone call to a key legislator in the House—may tip the scales towards freedom. You could be that person. There could be a dog trapped in a Marshall cage waiting for you to act. You won’t have to do it alone. I hope you’ll join us tomorrow. Pocan and Langworthy’s legislation is crucial, but it is just the beginning. We save the Marshall dogs next, building on the momentum behind the COMPACT Act. But after the Marshall dogs, we move to our greater mission: Save them all.

title: A Wisconsin Sheriff Sent This Puppy Back to His Abuser. He Broke the Law.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: Earlier this year, officers with a Wisconsin sheriff’s office came across a frightened puppy rescued from a dog fighting ring. They were faced with a question: what should we do with this traumatized dog? There was no dispute that the dog fighting ring had broken the law. State agencies investigating the ring had concluded the puppy’s “owners” were engaged in felony animal abuse that had left hundreds of dogs mutilated or dead. Indeed, the ring had secretly continued fighting dogs even when it had been ordered to stop. In March 2025, a legal order commanded the ring’s operators to end the illegal dog fights after whistleblowers came forward with allegations of criminal conduct. Yet an inspector visiting the site in September 2025 concluded that 150 more dogs had illegally been subjected to dog fights. The inspector concluded in a written order that “public health, safety, or welfare imperatively requires emergency action.” The inspector’s agency then sent a letter to the local law enforcement titled “Request for prosecution” and asked for their help in protecting the dogs. But law enforcement, including the Sheriff, took no action. Instead, they falsely claimed the dog fighter was above the law. There was an exception to the animal cruelty laws, the Sheriff claimed, for dog fighters that were doing research on dogs. And this particular operation claimed to have research on site. A sheriff deputy shoved a puppy into the back of his police cruiser. The Sheriff’s position was “absurd,” in the words of one prominent professor of criminal law. The existence of research on site, even if true, had no relevance to whether dog fighting is a crime. It was akin to the Sheriff saying that marijuana had been legalized—so a drug gang could not be prosecuted for murder. The Sheriff’s office was put on notice that his position was wrong: in a sworn declaration of the leading academic authority on the subject, by two state agencies, and even by a prosecutor who had previously worked on the case. The only party that had ever taken the Sheriff’s “absurd” position was the dog fighting ring itself (which, it was later discovered, had extensive ties to law enforcement). Indeed, the very “Request for prosecution” sent by the inspector made clear the Sheriff’s position was wrong. “This request for prosecution does not involve… bona fide research activities and operations,” the inspector wrote. Yet still, the Sheriff refused to act. Until he was forced to by private citizens taking direct action. Sheriff’s deputies came across a rescue van with a traumatized dog taken from the dog fighting ring. They arrested the driver for theft, and took custody of the dog and seven others rescued from abuse. This new scenario was, legally, very different. An officer who comes across an animal who may be a victim of criminal abuse (or other evidence of a crime) is legally required to hold them “so long as necessary for the purpose of being produced as evidence on any trial.” Further, the state and federal constitution require preservation of evidence that may be relevant to a criminal case; by arresting the driver, the Sheriff had triggered these constitutional rights and the duty to preserve the dog as evidence. But even these constitutional safeguards fell. The Sheriff chose to send this trembling puppy back to his abusers, where he knew he could be torn apart in a dog fight. By doing so—by violating numerous laws and bringing a victim to a known abuser—the Sheriff moved from inaction to criminal misconduct. Wisconsin law makes it a crime to provide assistance to someone you know to be committing acts of animal abuse. By doing so, you become “party to a crime.” The Sheriff consciously chose to do this. Then, he trumpeted his actions on his website. This story may sound comically evil or far-fetched. It is not. It is the exact scenario that unfolded over the last few months in Dane County, Wisconsin—with one small difference. The operation in question was not a dog fighter, but a dog testing and breeding facility called Ridglan Farms. Otherwise, every word, date, and quote by a legal expert is taken exactly from the Ridglan case, including the return of a frightened puppy to his abuser. (In this video on the I’ve Had It podcast, I refer to the dog as a girl, but we later realized he was a boy.) State authorities ordered Ridglan to stop the illegal surgeries performed by non-veterinarians without anesthesia in March 2025, after whistleblowers came forward. When inspectors came back to Ridglan in September, they found evidence that at least 150 more improper surgeries had occurred, despite the order to stop, and wrote that “public health, safety, or welfare imperatively requires emergency action.” They then referred the case to the local authorities for prosecution, listing out a long history of repeat violations at Ridglan Farms beyond the surgical mutilation of dogs, and explained why the research exception did not apply. But the Dane County authorities refused to prosecute or even investigate. Instead, they protected the abuser in ways that violated Wisconsin law. The most flagrant example of this was unlawfully delivering a traumatized puppy back to his abuser, along with 7 other frightened dogs. The animal cruelty laws, in short, were not just ignored by the authorities. They were broken. It’s time for that to change. Today, I and dozens of others will be walking into the Dane County District Attorney’s office with this criminal complaint . The complaint alleges three offenses against the local Sheriff, Kalvin Barrett: felony animal mistreatment; misconduct in public office; and harboring or aiding a felon (i.e., Ridglan Farms). I won’t bore you with the legal details, but I can tell you that this complaint has been vetted by many lawyers and is strong. But our purpose is not to send anyone to jail, or even convict anyone of a crime. What we need is a promise. A promise that animal cruelty laws will be enforced, impartially. A promise that industry influence will not corrupt the legal process. A promise that, the next time a frightened puppy comes into the hands of law enforcement, he won’t be sent back to his abuser to face torture and death. He will be rescued, as is his legal right. It won’t be easy to get that promise. It wasn’t easy the last time we filed a criminal complaint, accusing Ridglan itself of crimes. Many people, including prominent animal lawyers, told us that our petition was somewhere between improbable and crazy. “The industry is powerful,” they said. “The government? Corrupt.” But I think the puppy who was sent back to Ridglan is counting on us to seek accountability, even when it’s hard. I don’t know what came of that dog. Some of my fellow activists are certain that he was later saved. I hope they’re right. (I sometimes dream of him in a backyard with his family, playing tug of war and getting belly rubs. It brings me to tears.) What I do know is this: even if he’s gone, we can’t let his story die.

title: They Promised Him a Good Death. New Evidence Shows They Lied.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: A beagle at Marshall BioResources in North Rose, New York. The little lab beagle had nothing in life: no family, no walks, not even a soft place to lie down when he was in pain. But after a lifetime in a metal cage, he was at least promised this: no suffering in death. Even that small promise, however, was broken. On his last day on Earth, the frightened dog was stomped on the neck and injected with a toxic chemical into his belly. His death would not be a good death. It would be slow and agonizing, as the chemical burned him alive from the inside. Today, we submitted disturbing new evidence to New York authorities regarding the abuse of dogs at Marshall BioResources, the largest provider of dogs for experiments in the nation. The evidence, which is based on inspection records, photographic evidence, and new whistleblower accounts, is summarized in a criminal referral letter drafted by a former federal prosecutor, Bonnie Klapper , who spent a career pursuing violent drug cartels and knows a criminal enterprise when she sees one. And Klapper’s referral shows that dogs are killed at Marshall in ways that are so “depraved or sadistic” that they constitute felony abuse. Klapper asks Wayne County District Attorney, Christine Callanan, to immediately “open a criminal investigation” and “seize and protect animals” who face imminent torture or death. In a typical year, hundreds of dogs at Marshall are killed for a kink in the tail, the wrong-colored eyes, or even a mother dog acting too protectively toward her puppies. One dog, frightened and barking at staff, was stomped on the neck as sodium pentobarbital, a highly toxic chemical, was injected into his abdomen because the staff could not find a vein in his leg. When sodium pentobarbital is improperly injected into the belly, it causes dogs to thrash and scream for 5-10 minutes before they die. The dogs looked as if “they were being burned alive from the inside,” according to a witness to the killings. A dog being prepared for toxic inhalation experiments struggles under restraint. Another dog was strapped to a table for so-called inhalation training—a practice where dogs are forced to wear a face mask that will teach them to accept breathing deadly gases, including a chemical agent banned as a literal weapon of mass destruction. The dog tried to “alligator roll” to escape this torment but became tangled in the harness. She defecated and urinated in a panic and struggled against her restraints. When staff members found her, she was already dead. In a typical week, so many dogs were killed that the bags waiting for the incinerator stood as tall as the men stacking them. But the killings are just one part of Klapper’s body of evidence. Here are some of the others: Dogs being thrown like frisbees into cage walls so violently that it left the dogs’ jaws and heads shaking; Conditions so filthy that staff would engage in “panic cleans” before supposedly “unannounced” inspections by regulators; and Puppies suffocating to death in food pans, as they desperately searched for warmth on cold winter days by burying themselves in warm bowls dropped in their cages. An image from a Marshall BioResources facility in the United Kingdom. This conduct is not just cruel. It’s illegal. New York law makes it a crime when anyone “engages in… any act of cruelty.” That elevates to a felony when a dog is killed in a fashion that is “depraved or sadistic.” Marshall, in other words, is a criminal enterprise. So why has the government failed to stop its abuses? It’s not because the evidence was particularly hard to find. Evidence of abuse, including leaked photos and video , has been all over the internet in the last couple years. It is an open secret that Marshall abuses dogs. It’s also not because there are significant legal obstacles. There are clear provisions under state and federal law that give the government the immediate authority —indeed, the duty —to save the dogs. The reason the government has failed to protect the dogs is that it sees its abusers as “customers.” Internal strategy documents from the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, the government’s primary inspection agency for animal welfare, show the government describing animal abusers as “customers” to serve rather than corporations to hold accountable to the law. This bizarre state of affairs has not stopped Marshall from claiming they are “highly regulated and subject to ongoing oversight.” Indeed, in the last few days, the company has been posting incessantly on social media that government inspectors recently gave them a “clean report with no citations” after an “unannounced inspection.” (Marshall conveniently left out that the government has acknowledged that its inspections are “basically meaningless.”) For a long time, Marshall got away with these lies. But no longer. Klapper’s letter is the first stage in the truth coming out. Over the next few months, there will be more stories about the atrocities committed by Marshall BioResources against defenseless dogs. More importantly, there will be action. National political allies of our movement, such as Representative Nick Langworthy, are moving to pass legislation to protect the dogs. Protests are unfolding across the nation asking Marshall’s buyers to stop paying for criminal abuse of dogs. And in just a couple weeks, hundreds of people will be marching right up to the doorstep of Marshall . Nothing we do now helps the beagle who died screaming as brutal men stomped his neck. But everything we do now will determine what happens to the dogs that are left. So let’s go save the dogs. What you can do Call District Attorney Christine Callanan and Attorney General Letitia James and ask them to rescue the dogs . Both of these elected officials have the authority today to save every one of the Marshall dogs. Our web portal gives you all the info you need. Take action here . Join us in Wisconsin this weekend as we prepare for the next rescue effort . Whether through government intervention or direct citizen action, we will save these dogs. And there’s no better place to learn how to do this than the place where we did it last: Wisconsin, the home of Ridglan Farms. Register here . The March to Abolish Animal Testing will take hundreds right to the doorstep of Marshall in just a couple weeks—and we want you there with us. The government rarely takes action on cruelty complaints, as the Ridglan case demonstrates. But we can overcome that problem by putting pressure on them to enforce the law. On Sept. 12, we will begin our 207-mile march across New York, culminating on Sept. 26 with a massive rally at the gates of Marshall BioResources. Join us for a day, a mile, or all 207 . If you are a Marshall whistleblower, we are here to support you . More people are stepping up to share their stories of abuse. We have a world class legal team to help. Feel free to email me at this newsletter—or reach out via Direct Action Everywhere’s whistleblower helpline .

title: Stupidity Hurts Animals More Than Malice
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: The absurd response by Dane County authorities to the Ridglan rescue included tear gas and rubber bullets. “Stupidity is a more dangerous enemy of the good than malice.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote those words from a Nazi prison cell, two years before they hanged him. And his words have been on my mind. You see, the company executives and politicians who supported the abuse at Ridglan Farms didn’t usually seem malicious. Take Kalvin Barrett, the Sheriff of Dane County. When I spoke to him on the phone after the March rescue, he was friendly. You could have never guessed that he’d later task his officers with brutally assaulting peaceful rescuers. What’s unmistakable about the call with Barrett, instead, is that it’s… stupid. Barrett told me, in the tone of a man who sounds weirdly like a TV weatherman, that Ridglan was exempt from the animal cruelty laws. It is not. No statute says so. I had to stop myself from laughing. Bonhoeffer had similar interactions with members of the Nazi regime. He wrote: Against stupidity we are defenseless. Neither protests nor the use of force accomplish anything here; reasons fall on deaf ears; facts that contradict one’s prejudgment simply need not be believed — in such moments the stupid person even becomes critical — and when facts are irrefutable, they are just pushed aside as inconsequential, as incidental. In all this the stupid person, in contrast to the malicious one, is utterly self-satisfied and, being easily irritated, becomes dangerous by going on the attack. Bonhoeffer learned this lesson at the cost of his own life. But this stupidity is not individual. It’s social — more virus than trait. Bonhoeffer wrote: [It] is not so much that stupidity is a congenital defect, but that, under certain circumstances, people are made stupid… [P]ower in the public sphere, be it of a political or of a religious nature, infects a large part of humankind with stupidity. Stupidity of this sort, Bonhoeffer explained, was the result of power and blind obedience. And that’s exactly what happened with Ridglan Farms. Kalvin Barrett is not a mean man, and perhaps not a dumb man, either. But he is a blindly obedient one. And when he was told by the powerful people in Dane County that Ridglan was exempt from the animal cruelty laws, he accepted this position—even when it was clearly stupid and wrong. But here is the hardest part. The same is true of all of us. For years, I was too scared to rescue animals. I believed the “experts” who told me it was impossible. I was frightened by the state’s threats of punishment. So I blindly obeyed, even when my own reading of the law told me otherwise. I was stupid. And the animals suffered as a result. We are now changing that. Over 1,000 people showed up at Ridglan to fight a stupid system. And it collapsed. And that’s the thing about stupid systems: if enough people push against them, they always fall. That is the ultimate lesson of Bonhoeffer’s life. The stupidity of Nazism was its downfall. You cannot build a system on blind obedience. The Sheriffs of the world can tell us these animals must be tortured. Over the long run, the people won’t accept it. And once they rise up, the stupid will fall. Speaking of which, there’s no better place to learn to fight stupidity than the upcoming Save the Dogs Summit in Wisconsin from Sept 4-6 . And today is the last day for early-bird registration! Here’s a provisional schedule that will show you what we’re going to be up to. And here are five reasons we NEED you there. Reason 1: 16,000 dogs are facing sickening abuse at Marshall, including being bred for toxic inhalation studies. This is the summit where we’ll prep you to get them out. Reason 2: To succeed at the next rescue, we need to defend the last one. Just days before the summit, 47 new defendants will be charged with serious crimes. We need to support them—and set a precedent for the right to rescue that is heard across the nation. Reason 3: New evidence of criminal abuse will be revealed shortly. We want to share this info with you, and strategize together on how we can make sure it has maximum impact on saving the dogs. Reason 4: We’ll be deploying novel AI-empowered training methods—and teaching you to harness those methods to train others. From a mock trial to astonishing new research techniques, you’ll learn about powerful methods that have never been used before. Reason 5: You’ll be around some of the most inspiring dog rescuers in the world. It’s not just the 51 defendants but the 100s of others who risked everything to save the dogs. We are stronger together. You’ll see that—feel that—if you come to the summit! See you in Madison !

title: The Last Ridglan Beagle Is Free. So Why Am I in Despair?
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: A beagle trapped in a cage at Ridglan Farms on March 15. The last 150 beagles from Ridglan were released on Wednesday; every last dog is now free. We’ve established a solid strategy for defending the 47 new defendants who face charges for the rescue, including the Save the Dogs Summit , where we’ll gather to support them in Wisconsin from Sept 4-6. (Heads up: early bird pricing ends tomorrow!) And we just received fascinating new documents about the police response on April 18 that will help us with the next rescue effort. (More on that in a bit.) It’s been a week of great news. So you might be surprised to hear that I’ve been feeling despair. While the dogs are free, it should not have been this hard to get the government to enforce the law. The evidence against Ridglan was overwhelming. And yet the government has doubled down on cruelty by pursuing the largest prosecution of animal rescuers in history while doing nothing to hold animal abusers to account. Some days I look at all of it and think: what is the point? The system is fucked. But when I start feeling this way, I remind myself of the story of Martin Seligman. Seligman is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, where he made one of the most famous discoveries in the history of psychology . And he did it by electrocuting a dog. In the experiment, Seligman placed a dog in a “shuttle box” with two compartments and metal flooring from which he could deliver painful shocks. One side was electrified; the other, a short barrier away, was not. And when a shock was delivered, Seligman noted that the dog “runs frantically about, defecating, urinating, and howling, until it accidentally scrambles over the barrier and so escapes the shock.” All the dogs eventually learned to jump to the safe side of the box to avoid the shock. But there was an exception. When dogs were placed in a shuttle box where electric shocks were initially delivered to both sides of the box, they would run just as frantically but find no safety. Soon, they would simply lie down on the floor, whining helplessly, as they were repeatedly shocked. Remarkably, this would continue even when the electricity on one side of the box was turned off. There was an easy way to escape the shocks—just jump to the other side of the box—but the dogs had given up. Seligman called it “learned helplessness.” Teach an animal that her efforts are futile, and she loses the ability to see the way out even when it’s just inches away. Seligman’s goal in the experiment was to understand human despair. He succeeded at that—his work is celebrated across the field of psychology—but he failed to grasp the moral stain in his work: He had reached a breakthrough in understanding human despair by causing despair in dogs. There is nothing to celebrate in that. But I’m not sharing this story to tarnish an old professor’s reputation. I share it because the pathology Seligman saw in dogs—learned helplessness—extends to the humans who love dogs as well. We have been taught to be helpless in the face of cruel shocks. This is true of me. I remember when I first learned that dogs from Ridglan had been force-fed industrial laundry detergent . I was shocked. I had to save these dogs. But for 10 years, the system tried to teach me that it was hopeless to try. I filed a criminal complaint . No one responded. I worked with a journalist to expose the conditions. It was ignored. And when I finally walked right into Ridglan in April 2017, and came out with a blind, frightened puppy—little Julie—the government charged me with crimes. As the case proceeded, many told me to give up. “Take a plea,” one experienced leader in the movement told me. “Live to fight another day.” And there were days when that was tempting. But I refused to accept that we were helpless. Maybe we couldn’t rescue all the dogs ourselves. But I thought we could win people over to this cause. So we fought. We did small things. A press release. A ten-person protest. Another letter to a politician. Each was insignificant on its own. Each was still a win. And something amazing happened. The momentum started to build, with sympathetic portrayals in the media. Social media videos started going viral. Then, on the first morning of trial, the government dropped every charge against me and my co-defendants. That win taught thousands of people that we can beat the industry. We can rescue the dogs and win in court. And on April 18, 1000+ people marched right up to Ridglan to bring that lesson to life. Now Ridglan is finished. Its victims will no longer face torture in a vivisector’s cage. They’ll grow old with their families. And it happened because we fought back against learned helplessness. There is a lesson here, one that Seligman himself later discovered . If you feel helpless, find small ways to make progress—then do these small things over and over until you have taught yourself that you can make a difference. Seligman calls it “the expectation of control,” but I think there’s a better term: learned strength . We have to teach ourselves—and one another—that we have the strength to help. And now we have to learn that lesson again. There are big obstacles ahead. Our friends face serious criminal charges, including up to 15 years in prison. RFK Jr. and Brooke Rollins made big commitments—to phase out animal experiments—but have yet to deliver on their promises . Most importantly, tens of thousands of dogs remain trapped in laboratory cages, victims of criminal abuse like the phosgene gas experiments inflicted on beagles from Marshall BioResources . In the face of so much cruelty and corruption, it would be easy to learn to be helpless. But we can’t let that happen. We have to learn to find strength, even in seemingly small actions. The phone call to a legislator. The dinner with a friend who tears up about the dogs. The video of the Ridglan pups that goes on social media. Every step is building our capacity. It’s teaching us to be strong. That, more than anything, is what we will do at the Save the Dogs Summit: learn strength. The road ahead is a hard one. It would be easy to give up. But we have to see the opportunities, even in adversity. We’ll do that in Madison from Sept 4-6—and create a movement stronger than it’s ever been. Then, we’ll save all the dogs. Other stuff The Save the Dogs Summit is happening on Sept 4-6 in Madison, WI, and early bird registration ends tomorrow. We’ll be sharing new disturbing evidence of criminal abuse at some of the largest vivisection facilities in the nation—and giving you the practical skills to make “small wins” for the dogs. Just as important, we’ll be holding a rally in defense of the Ridglan rescue on the first day of the summit. Sign up here! If you can come early to the summit, attend the preliminary hearing on Sept 2. Forty-seven new defendants face charges, and the evidence will be presented against them for the first time in court. When the courtroom is packed for the rescuers, it changes the entire tone of the proceeding—and helps us gain favorable media. I’ll be there in court. I hope you will, too. We are holding our usual weekly call for the Save the Dogs Network on Saturday at 1 pm ET / 10 am PT, and I’ll be sharing some important new evidence we’ve obtained about the police actions on April 18. If you recall, the police used military-style force against peaceful rescuers on that day. And we’ve just obtained internal policy memos on the nature of that police response, which I’ll break down with you tomorrow. Jen will also be sharing some new opportunities to reach legislators, and Ella will talk about updates on the March to Abolish Animal Testing. Here’s the link .

title: Why Fauci Lied About Funding the Torture of Dogs
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: “These beagle puppies… have their throats slit!” On June 3, 2024, Rep. Nicole Malliotakis accused Dr. Anthony Fauci and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) of funding horrific animal abuse: torturing beagles and bunnies in experiments; injecting dogs with ticks; and even slitting puppies’ throats. “With all due respect, I’m not sure what you’re talking about,” Fauci responded. “The experiments go through strict regulatory processes of the humane treatment of animals.” The allegations of animal abuse made against Fauci have been mocked by the media. Prominent newspapers such as The Washington Post have described them as right-wing conspiracy theories. But this week, the watchdog group White Coat Waste (WCW) dropped proof on social media that it was Fauci, and not Malliotakis, who lied. In an invoice WCW published on X/Twitter , the NIH is shown to be paying for 46 “cordectomies”—the slitting of a dog’s vocal cords. The procedure, which has been criticized by the American Veterinary Medical Association because of the risk of “[b]leeding, acute airway swelling, infection, coughing, gagging and aspiration pneumonia,” was not performed for any medical purpose. Rather, by the NIH’s own admission , it was done to “reduce noise” in a facility packed with distressed dogs. The vivisectors didn’t want to hear the beagles cry while they were force-fed experimental drugs. And the name of the company paid to engage in this brutal practice? None other than Marshall BioResources , which violated New York’s animal cruelty law , which bans unjustifiably mutilating an animal, by performing the cordectomies. WCW’s evidence shows indisputably that the payments to Marshall were part of a $1.68 million grant from the NIH. And even The Washington Post now acknowledges that the NIH funded beagle experiments—and attempted to hide it by claiming it was a right-wing conspiracy theory. The invoice to the NIH showing surgical mutilation of dogs’ vocal cords at Marshall BioResources. Join the Save the Dogs Summit in Madison, WI from Sept 4-6 as we share essential skills to rescue the Marshall dogs! The NIH beagle controversy, however, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to government cover-ups of animal abuse. Over the last few decades, the government has systematically conspired with corporations to break the law in order to sustain an abusive industry. Consider this: while Fauci testified about the strict regulatory processes and humane standards in animal experiments, the government’s own internal watchdog, the Inspector General (IG), concluded that the enforcement of those humane standards was “basically meaningless.” The IG condemned the USDA for partnering with animal abusers—e.g., waiving fines and illegally redirecting those penalties into reinvestments into cruel facilities—rather than holding them accountable. And yet in the last few years, enforcement of welfare standards has somehow gotten even worse. There was just 1 fine for violating the Animal Welfare Act (out of the millions of protected animals) in the first 7 months of 2025, a dramatic decline from the dozens in a typical year—already a very low figure. Fauci repeatedly defended animal experiments as “strictly regulated” even as he knew (or should have known) enforcement was going from meaningless to nonexistent. It’s as if the Mayor of New York City wrote one parking ticket in 2025 then proclaimed his city was free of crime. Why does the government lie about animal abuse? The influence of money is part of the answer. The enforcement system for animal welfare laws is a classic example of what’s called regulatory capture, a process by which an industry takes over its supposed government regulators. Over $10 billion in federal taxpayer dollars goes into the animal testing industry annually, and contractors , lobbyists , and even private security companies go back and forth between industry and government positions. These ties are apparent with Anthony Fauci. When he was given the Legend in Leadership award at Yale University in 2021, it was the CEOs of Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson—companies that have been implicated in abusive animal experiments—who presented him the award. Fauci was part of a government that should have been “strictly regulating” these companies. But it would be impolite to accuse pharma CEOs of animal abuse when they are bestowing you a lavish award. But there is another and more important reason the government covers up the abuse: they’ve never faced consequences for lying. While animal advocates have complained about cruel experiments for decades, those responsible for the abuses never faced any penalties. Anthony Fauci is an example of this. Fauci was co-author of a study that injected endangered chimpanzees with the HIV virus in 1984. HIV experiments of this sort were condemned by AIDS researchers and primatologists, including Jane Goodall, as profoundly unethical, and the government eventually phased out the funding . But Fauci never faced any career consequences. To the contrary, he rose to the pinnacle of his field, overseeing billions in grants for the same unethical animal experiments he himself performed on chimps. But that is now changing. Malliotakis’s grilling of Fauci shows that animal abuse is now a political liability. (Fauci’s recently-released diary shows that, when former President Barack Obama called him in 2021, one of his main complaints to Obama was that people were calling him a puppy killer.) Similarly, the politicians who covered up animal abuse in Wisconsin at Ridglan Farms—District Attorney Ismael Ozanne and Sheriff Kalvin Barrett—are now among the most loathed elected officials in the state. Sheriff Barrett’s Facebook page is filled with people condemning him for supporting the torture of dogs. That bodes well for the future. Anthony Fauci rose to the highest levels of government power, while lying about the abuse of animals in labs. But he will be among the last of his kind. The truth eventually comes out. The public doesn’t want our government funding animal torture. It wants our government to stop it. Other stuff You will not want to miss the Save the Dogs summit from Sept 4-6 . We can save the dogs at Marshall, and around the nation. But we will need you trained to be the best activist you can be. This summit will be indispensable, as we’ll be doing hands-on workshops on how you can help save the dogs. This includes an immediate opportunity: preparing you for the March to Abolish Animal Testing which starts on September 12 in Albany, NY and ends on September 26 at Marshall’s massive facility in North Rose, NY. Preliminary hearings for the 51 Ridglan defendants will be on Sept 2. If you can come early to the summit, join the courtroom mobilization as we defend the rescuers who saved dogs from Ridglan Farms, and push for a precedent for the right to rescue. We are now holding weekly all-network Zoom calls on Saturdays at 1 pm ET / 10 am PT. This week, I’ll be discussing the revelation that the NIH funded cordectomies at Marshall—and how we plan to use this and other evidence to press the government to save all the 16,000+ dogs trapped in cages at their facility. We will need your help! Here’s the link for today’s call . That’s all for now!

title: March for the Kitten Who Couldn’t
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: Kittens being raised for use in experiments. Tucked away in a little-read inspection report is the story of a kitten whose tail was chewed down to the bone. The male kitten was noted as having a serious injury to his tail on March 26, 2023, when he was still with his mom and siblings in a cage at Marshall BioResources. But instead of keeping him with his mom, Marshall threw the frightened boy into an enclosure with other male cats. Records at the facility noted that the other animals quickly converged on the injured kitten and left his injured tail “chewed to the bone.” With his mother gone, and metal walls trapping him in the enclosure, he had no way to protect himself or escape. Marshall killed him on the same day. A mutilated and traumatized cat would have no value in experiments. Join me and hundreds of other activists in marching against animal experiments starting on September 12. The signup form is here . We value our freedoms greatly in this nation. The freedom to speak. To worship. To pursue happiness. But the freedom to move is perhaps the one we neglect the most. It’s so basic it’s hard to imagine life without it. Without that freedom, we can’t find food, seek safer shelter, or even escape from those who might hurt us. And yet freedom of movement is just one of the many that the animals of Marshall are denied. In the case of this small kitten, that led to a violent death. In the case of so many others, including 16,000 beagles, it leads at best to a life hardly worth living. Life in a laboratory cage. It’s for that reason that the March to Abolish Animal Testing feels so poignant. Hundreds of people, including me, will exercise their freedom to take a 200 mile trek from the state capital in Albany to the doorstep of Marshall starting on September 12. One thousand are anticipated to rally on the last day of the march at the gates of the very company where that kitten died. And we will exercise their freedom to move because the animals can’t. We will ask the authorities: How can you justify letting kittens and puppies be brutalized? The authorities, needless to say, would rather ignore all of this. Marshall is one of the largest employers in the county. As a multinational corporation with facilities in Asia and Europe, as well as the US, its influence is global. Elected figures in the state of New York, and in the local county, have been beholden to its power. Especially in Wayne County, the small county in which Marshall is located, that remains the case. Recent news articles include quotes from Sheriff and House representative defending Marshall and threatening advocates with criminal charges. And yet something is changing. For the first time in history, Congress members, even in the area, are speaking out. House Rep. Nick Langworthy showed up at the doorstep of Marshall himself a few weeks ago, only to get the same response that animal advocates get: a call to security. Social media posts about Marshall are going viral. A typical protest for animal rights, even dogs, is lucky to get a few thousand views. The protests of Marshall and its buyers are often getting millions. But something else is stirring that shows Marshall’s power is weakening. The people are acting. It’s not just a few politicians or influencers on social media. It’s everyone. Demonstrations at Marshall, a remote region of New York, are getting larger every year. Media coverage is growing, and more positive. The March from Albany to Marshall will be a way to harness that sympathy into something concrete: 1000 people standing outside the gates asking for the animals to be freed. There will be much more said and written about this effort. There are powerful parallels to marches from history, from Selma to the Salt March. But for now, I just want to invite you to join us. I will be there on the first day, asking the Attorney General and Governor of New York to enforce the law and protect the dogs. We don’t know how they will respond, but we know we are on the right side of history. And as more people join our march to freedom, it will become obvious to everyone that this is the case—and the animals at Marshall will be freed. I hope you’ll join us in Albany on September 12. —- Other Stuff Our strategy to save the dogs is pivoting—and we’ll be talking about it at a call on Sunday at 3 pm ET / 12 pm PT. We’ll discuss two promising new developments that could change the timeline of our rescue effort. RSVP here . Don’t forget to log in to our activist portal and contact your Congress members about the USDA’s inaction at Marshall . The link is app.savethedogs.io , and it will give you easy instructions on how you can help. The right to rescue summit is moving forward on the weekend of September 5. The exact schedule will be worked out soon. Stay tuned! That’s all for now!

title: Two Legislators Are Trying to Save Beagles from Being Gassed to Death. They Need Your Help.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: A Marshall beagle being prepared for inhalation experiments. You would think the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) would be concerned about dogs being gassed to death with chemical weapons banned under international law , given its responsibility to enforce animal welfare laws. You would think this would be doubly true if two prominent Congressmembers, including one who is a member of the committee with investigative powers over federal agencies , demanded them to act. And you would be wrong. Because the USDA—the institution tasked with protecting animals—has been captured by the industries that abuse them. Reach out to your Congressional representatives and ask them to tell the USDA to help the animals suffering criminal abuse at Marshall BioResources. Here are instructions for doing that! On June 26, 2026, House Reps. Nick Langworthy and Rep. Nicole Malliotakis wrote to the head of the USDA asking for basic information about federal inspections at the largest dog and cat breeding and experimentation facility in the nation, Marshall BioResources of North Rose, New York. Their request comes in the wake of years of damning disclosures about Marshall. In August 2021, federal inspectors found a series of animals with serious and untreated injuries, including one mama with a puncture wound in her mammary gland. In May 2023, they found a kitten whose tail had been “chewed to the bone” after being injured and forced to live in a cage with aggressive animals who attacked him. And in September 2024, whistleblower footage was published showing dogs being trained for so-called “inhalation experiments.” The dogs would thrash on a table, desperately trying to escape the black masks that would soon feed them poisoned gas. A published study showed the purpose of this training protocol. Marshall beagles were being forced to breathe phosgene gas, a chemical weapon banned by the Geneva Protocol after killing 70,000+ people in World War I . The inhalation training was meant to teach them it was pointless to struggle, even as the phosgene gas ate away at their lungs. Yet despite this evidence of criminal abuse, the USDA has to date refused to lift a finger to help the dogs. Animal advocates have for years complained that the USDA is letting facilities like Marshall get away with breaking the law, including the federal PACT Act (which prohibits causing serious bodily injury to animals) and the Animal Welfare Act (which requires adequate veterinary care). Indeed, the USDA’s own internal watchdog, the Inspector General, has admitted for decades that its enforcement mechanisms are “basically meaningless” and that its own inspectors often act in cahoots with the agency. But the USDA’s latest action, ignoring the legal demands of two sitting House members, is perhaps its most brazen yet. Rep. Langworthy is a member of the powerful House Oversight Committee, expressly commissioned to investigate federal agencies for misconduct. He has worked with Rep. Mark Pocan, one of the most progressive members of Congress, to push for greater oversight over experiments on dogs. But even Langworthy apparently has no power to stop the USDA and Marshall from acting with impunity. The deadline in Langworthy’s letter passed without so much as a word from the USDA. There is a simple reason for this: legalized corruption. For decades, the USDA has been a revolving door for the industry it supposedly regulates. USDA chiefs from both parties are guaranteed cushy jobs or sweetheart deals with 7-figure payouts when they’re done with their government service. More generally, up and down the USDA’s power structure, the industry has embedded itself in the very agency that is supposed to protect the public (and animals) from its abuses. The noted lawyers Mariann Sullivan and David Wolfson have described this as “foxes” guarding the “henhouse.” But Langworthy’s letter shows that this corrupt scheme is breaking. Powerful legislators are demanding accountability from the USDA, perhaps for the first time in history. And driving this accountability is public support for their actions. Langworthy’s posts on social media about fighting for the beagles are going viral. One post on Langworthy’s X/Twitter page has 148,000 views—10x the engagement he usually gets. If Langworthy and other politicians continue to go viral for helping the dogs—including, in Langworthy’s case, literally going to Marshall’s doorstep to demand freedom for the beagles—it will set a political precedent for other legislators to follow. This is why today’s deadline is so important. The USDA is not just blowing off two House members. It is blowing off our democracy. But if more House members speak out—a mere 7 members of the House Oversight Committee can issue a subpoena forcing action—then we can expose the cruelty and corruption at the USDA and inspire action to save the dogs. And, importantly, you can help us make that happen. Every federal legislator has the power to join Langworthy and Malliotakis in their demand of the USDA. Every US resident has at least 3 legislators—a House representative and two Senators—who are responsible to you. If enough people make calls, post on social media, and push our legislators to act, we can save the Marshall dogs. But we need people like you to step up. Here’s how . Other stuff We are revamping our strategy to challenge the dog experimentation industry in light of the additional charges filed against 47 rescues from Ridglan . The trials of the beagle rescuers are an immense opportunity to raise attention to the cause—and defend the right to rescue. So we’re probably going to be reorganizing our strategy towards a defense of rescue in the next few months, including a summit that will be organized around Sept 5-6 in Madison, Wisconsin. That does not mean we are letting Marshall off the hook. The next few months will be an important time to continue to educate the public—and the authorities—about the illegal actions routinely taken by mass confinement facilities such as Marshall. The goal will be to push the system to do the right thing and save the dogs. My friends at the International Council for Animal Welfare just released a disturbing investigation of battery cages at Kroger, one of the nation’s largest grocers . The video footage is not for the faint of heart. But it’s important for anyone to realize what these corporations are flat out lying to the public. Kroger promised years ago to ban practices that ICAW is now revealing to the public. I’d encourage everyone to sign their petition and take action. I’m looking for people in London to assist with a studio and podcast. I’m hoping to relaunch the podcast and start producing more video content. If you know someone who might be interested and has the right skillset—or, more importantly, extreme motivation to cultivate that skillset—let me know!

title: They're Charging 47 More People for the Ridglan Rescue. Here's Why We'll Win.
author: Wayne Hsiung
body: A frightened beagle dragged back to Ridglan on March 15. We still do not know what happened to her. On Independence Day, the Dane County authorities are defending tyranny. Yesterday, District Attorney Ismael Ozanne filed felony burglary charges against 47 additional people —teachers and firefighters, parents and lawyers—for the Ridglan rescue on March 15, bringing the total to 51 defendants. The timing was deeply ironic. Two-hundred and fifty years ago on this day, the founders of this nation dreamed in their Declaration of Independence of a nation that defended “Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.” Today, those who hold power will spend millions to defend a criminal industry that kills and cages desperate dogs. The Simple Heart is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. The distinguished philosopher Peter Singer called it a tyranny 50 years ago. And he was right. From the use of chemical weapons to the deadly force-feeding of laundry detergent , human beings rule these animals by fear. Now, with this new prosecution, corrupt actors within the government are trying to spread this fear through the movement of rescuers. Fifty-one people, many of whom have no criminal history and literally would not hurt a fly, will face serious felony charges for trying to save puppies from criminal torture or death. We begged Ozanne to enforce the law and protect the dogs. He promised to look into things; to review our evidence; or even just to return our calls. And over and over, he broke his promise—then decided to target us when we acted within our rights to save the dogs. The message Ozanne is sending, on behalf of the criminal enterprises that he represents 1 , is rule by fear: “You will comply, or you will pay.” It is truly a terrifying state of affairs—and one that has, for the last 20 years, radicalized my views on American government. We do not live in a functioning democracy. We do not even really live in a functioning state, at least when it comes to animals; that requires a state to follow its own rules. Even when we irrefutably demonstrate that the powerful are targeting the powerless with violent and criminal acts, the authorities refuse to stop them. And if you challenge this corruption, the powerful will target you, too. What is one to do? My first response to this was to reach out to the defendants and offer support. Many will be first-time defendants facing the terrifying power of a corrupt state apparatus. They will need us to back them and stay unified. All of us . If you know one of the defendants , reach out and offer them some support. But my second response was this: Bring it on. Because we are now ready to win this fight. We will no longer be ruled by fear. Twenty years ago, when the animal rights movement faced its first wave of serious prosecutions, it split and fell apart. The largest animal protection organizations condemned fellow activists as “terrorists.” Individual friendships were destroyed, and, in some cases, there was outright betrayal , as in the case of Justin Samuel, who testified against his fellow activists. Repression broke the movement. We had neither the strength nor the strategy to fight back. Heck, we could barely make it into court. That is no longer the case. Indeed, from Day 1 of our efforts at Ridglan, we planned for exactly this eventuality . The old divisions in the movement have been healed; I consider many in the more “moderate” parts of animal advocacy dear friends. The grassroots is unified; even when forces have tried to divide us, asking for cancelations and purity tests, we have stayed unified. And we have legal strategies that have won historic verdicts . That is why Ridglan’s first effort to prosecute us failed so spectacularly . We made the repression backfire. Now all the dogs are free. And we will do it again. But this time, we won’t just free the Ridglan dogs. We’ll free them all . There is much more to say about our strategy for making this happen. And you will hear me (and others) say it. But let me end this newsletter with a response to Ozanne’s message: “You will comply, or you will pay.” In another era, it would have worked. But no longer. Because this is what we say in reply: “We will rescue them, no matter what it takes.” It is a message of compassion. And in the battle between fear and compassion, compassion will win. Other stuff Support the defendants . We will be meeting with the defendants shortly to come up with a joint legal strategy. In the meantime, give these people some love . They risked everything to save the dogs—and succeeded. They need us to back them! Even just sharing this newsletter can make a difference! Conveniently, I was just on the Animal Law Podcast to discuss our recent (partial) victory for the right to rescue in the California Court of Appeals . An appellate court ruled that it was unlawful to forbid me from arguing that my intent was to save animals from criminal abuse in my trial from late 2023 . There’s a lot more detail in the podcast, especially for folks who like geeking out on the law. Check it out . The line prosecutor in the Ridlgan prosecution, Matthew Moeser, is illegally attempting to delay my trial while charging dozens of other defendants. Sadly, the trial court sided with the prosecutor in violation of my speedy trial rights. But we are appealing the judge’s order . I’m looking to potentially hire a “chief of staff” to help me handle operations and communications across a bunch of different organizational contexts. I’m pretty overwhelmed with logistics tasks (from finance to email management) and desperately need help. Send me an email with a CV if you’re interested. Experience is less important than intelligence, curiosity, and self-motivation—but I’m only looking to hire someone who is world-class in these areas! That’s all for now! 1 This is not a rhetorical flourish or personal attack. The only engagement Ozanne has had with the criminal allegations against Ridglan Farms was to sit with Ridglan’s attorney, Eric McLeod , when we presented evidence of criminal animal abuse in court.
